title: Horror
objective: After this level you can explain why audiences choose to be scared and how horror films build dread before the shock.
summary: A 2020 haunted-house study found enjoyment peaks at a just-right amount of fear. Cat People (1942) never shows its monster, letting shadows, silence and imagination build dread.

cards.headline: Why would anyone pay to be frightened?
cards.body: Britannica defines a horror film as one calculated to cause intense repugnance, fear or dread. That sounds like a product nobody would buy. Yet people line up for it. So researchers went into a haunted house to find out why.

cards.headline: A haunted house full of heart monitors
cards.body: In a 2020 study, researchers fitted 110 visitors to a commercial haunted house in Vejle, Denmark, with heart rate monitors, then asked how scared they felt and how much they enjoyed it. They were studying recreational fear: feeling fear and enjoyment at the same time. It sounds like a contradiction. Anyone who has laughed right after a scream knows it isn't.

cards.headline: Scared, but just right
cards.body: The results traced an upside-down U. Visitors who were barely scared enjoyed the house less, and so did those who were too scared. Enjoyment peaked at a just-right amount of fear. The researchers compare it to play: the fun comes from just-right departures from your body's normal state. Think of a horror film as a dial, and the filmmakers trying to leave it in the sweet spot.

cards.headline: The cat you never see
cards.body: Horror doesn't have to show its monster. Cat People (1942), produced by Val Lewton for RKO on a skeletal budget, never shows its heroine Irena in cat form. It relies on suggestion and your imagination: shadows and low lighting build the suspense, and silences are held long enough to turn into dread. Your imagination draws a scarier cat than any costume could.

mascot.line: Keep this: dread is the waiting, and it's built from what you can't quite see. Level 58 shows why knowing more makes waiting worse.

questions.prompt: In the 2020 haunted-house study, which visitors enjoyed the experience most?

options.label: Those who felt no fear at all
options.rationale: Barely scared visitors enjoyed it less.

options.label: Those who felt a just-right amount of fear
Those who were as scared as possible
options.rationale: Too much fear lowered enjoyment too.

options.label: Those who had never seen a horror film
options.rationale: The study tracked how scared people felt, not their viewing history.

questions.explanation: Enjoyment followed an upside-down U: it peaked at a just-right amount of fear.

questions.prompt: Horror promises fear, in line with Level 51's genre promise. By the haunted-house study, why can a horror film that barely frightens disappoint?

options.label: Too little fear lowers enjoyment, breaking the promise
Horror fans enjoy it only when they are terrified
options.rationale: Too much fear lowered enjoyment as well.

options.label: A genre promises only something completely new
options.rationale: A genre promises the familiar and the new.

options.label: Fear has no link to enjoyment
options.rationale: The study found a clear link: the upside-down U.

questions.explanation: Barely scared visitors enjoyed the haunted house less, so a horror film that fails to frighten fails to deliver what the genre promised.
